newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West urges talks to halt fissile material production.
newsitem.headline: West urges talks to halt fissile material production.

text.p: The Conference on Disarmament, which ended its 1996 session on Thursday, heard a final plea by Western states to begin substantive negotiations next year on a treaty to halt production of bomb-making fissile material.
Britain's envoy, Sir Michael Weston, who was speaking on behalf of the 21 states of the Western Group, hinted the Geneva forum should look at tackling a ban on anti-personnel landmines.
But diplomats said that the conference's future remained clouded as the 61 member states have yet to agree on a formal negotiating agenda for the 1997 session which opens in January.
Three states -- Canada, Australia and New Zealand -- broke ranks somewhat with Western allies on Thursday, calling for the body to go further and address wider nuclear disarmament issues.

The Non-Aligned Movement, led by India, are demanding that negotiations to halt production of fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium) be linked to an agreement to launch fresh talks in Geneva on nuclear disarmament.
The five declared nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France Russia and the United States -- have refused to make such a commitment, preferring a step-by-step approach to disarmament.
Some Western delegates fear that the non-aligned could hold the forum and the fissile negotiations hostage to its demands.
Weston noted the conference had agreed in March 1995 to negotiate a "cut-off" convention to halt production of fissile material, but that there had been no progress.
"Since then we have continued to urge the immediate commencement of these negotiations," Weston said in a speech.
"We firmly believe that the ad hoc committee should be established promptly," he added.

The three so-called "threshold states" with nuclear capability -- India, Pakistan and Israel -- are keen to continue their secret production of fissile material for as long as possible to build up stocks, according to Western diplomats.
However, they noted that as part of the so-called Western Group, Israel had gone along with Weston's carefully-drafted statement. "It will be hard for them to back away now from cut-off," said one.
Weston said the Western Group had "taken note with interest" of the remarks by Algeria's ambassador this month concerning a growing political will to launch negotiations on landmines.
Hocine Meghlaoui, Algeria's ambassador who serves as the conference's special coordinator on outstanding issues, referred to landmines in a speech on September 3.

"Opening such negotiations would permit our institution to brush up its tarnished image, leave time to pursue consultations on the agenda and lower the temperature which has been too high over the last months," he said.
President Clinton last May announced the United States would limit the use of anti-personnel landmines that do not self-destruct and would seek a global ban on all landmines by the year 2001.
However, Washington has yet to say in what forum it would like to see the landmines negotiations held.

The Conference on Disarmament adopted its annual report to the General Assembly, acknowledging it had failed to reach consensus on a nuclear test ban treaty -- finally agreed by the parent body in New York on Wednesday.
India blocked agreement on the test ban pact in the Geneva talks, the main U.N. disarmament negotiating forum, which spent more than two-and-half-years trying to clinch a deal.

Ludwik Dembinski, Poland's envoy who serves as conference chairman until January, agreed to hold intensive consultations over the next months to seek consensus on a formal agenda as well as requests by 14 more states to join.
"The agenda is a tough nut to crack," said a Western envoy. "Things look rather bleak. It would be a miracle by the middle of next year if the conference agrees to actually pursue something."
